newsitem.title: USA: Pfizer earnings held back by potent R&D spending.
newsitem.headline: Pfizer earnings held back by potent R&D spending.

text.p: Pfizer Inc net earnings rose 13 percent for the second quarter, but fell slightly short of Wall Street expectations as the company ramped up research and development in hopes of creating "waves" of new products in the next four years.

"We have a very strong, relatively new product portfolio now but are planning a second wave of three to four new drugs before the year 2000," Pfizer Chief Financial Officer David Shedlarz told Reuters late Tuesday.
The company's second-quarter earnings of $0.35 cent per share were one cent shy of First Call consensus estimate, restrained by the ambitious R&D program.

Overall year-on-year R&D expenses jumped nine percent to $461 million in the quarter, the company said, as new compounds advanced into expensive late stages of clinical trials and others proceeded through early-stage development.

Shedlarz said he expected the wave of new products to include quinolone antibiotic Trovan and the shizophrenia drug Zeldox, both of which are awaiting approvals from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

"Then there will be a third wave, with numerous additional drugs around the year 2000," Shedlarz said, repeating company forecasts that its research and development expenses this year would jump to $2 billion from $1.7 billion in 1996.

He said there was a "delicate balance" between quarterly earnings growth and the need to invest in R&D. "We're sensitive to that balance. But R&D is the lifeblood of our company. We've increased our earnings but intend to build our infrastructure," he said.
Barbara Ryan, an Alex. Brown & Sons pharmaceuticals analyst, forecast accurately that increased R&D expenses would hold Pfizer's earnings to $0.35 per share in the quarter.
"Pfizer will probably be the research and development leader this year," she said. "They have a lot of drugs in the pipeline and a lot in Phase III (pivotal) trials."
Ryan said history had taught Pfizer it was worthwhile to risk slightly lower earnings in the short term for healthy long-term growth.

"Over the last five years they've had spectacular payoff from R&D," she said, including Norvasc, Pfizer's hypertension and angina drug, which had sales of $521 million in the second quarter and which she expects to reach sales of $2.3 billion for the year.

Other recently introduced products include antidepressant Zoloft, which she expects will have 1997 sales of $1.6 billion, and broad-spectrum antibiotic Zithromax with possible sales of $800 million for the year.
Shares of Pfizer, which the New York Stock Exchange said were unavailable for after-hours trading, rose 15/16 to 61-1/2 before the release of the earnings report.
